landmarks.name: Ancient City of Babylon
landmarks.writeup: A historic city famous for its ancient ruins and the Hanging Gardens, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

wiki.extract: Babylon is an ancient city located on the lower Euphrates river in southern Mesopotamia, within modern-day Hillah, Iraq, about 85 kilometres south of modern-day Baghdad. Babylon functioned as the main cultural and political centre of the Akkadian-speaking region of Babylonia. Its rulers established two important empires in antiquity, the 19th–16th century BC Old Babylonian Empire, and the 7th–6th century BC Neo-Babylonian Empire. Babylon was also used as a regional capital of other empires, such as the Achaemenid Empire. Babylon was one of the most important urban centres of the ancient Near East, until its decline during the Hellenistic period. Nearby ancient sites include Kish, Borsippa, Dilbat, and Kutha.

landmarks.name: Al-Mustansiriya University
landmarks.writeup: One of the oldest universities in the world, established in Baghdad in the 13th century.

wiki.extract: Al-Mustansiriya University is a public university located in Baghdad, Iraq. It traces its origin back to 1227. The modern form of the university was founded in 1963.

landmarks.name: Erbil Citadel
landmarks.writeup: A continuously inhabited settlement and one of the oldest human-made structures in the world.

wiki.extract: The Citadel of Erbil, locally called Qellat, is a tell or occupied mound, and the historical city centre of Erbil in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq. The citadel was added to the World Heritage List on 21 June 2014.

landmarks.name: Great Mosque of Samarra
landmarks.writeup: Known for its unique spiral minaret, it was once the largest mosque in the world.

wiki.extract: The Great Mosque of Samarra or Al-Malwiya Mosque is a former congregational mosque, now in partial ruins, in Samarra, in the Saladin Governorate of Iraq. The mosque was commissioned in 848 CE and completed in 851 by the Abbasid caliph Al-Mutawakkil. At the time of construction it was the world's largest mosque. It is known for its 52-metre-high (171 ft) minaret encircled by a spiral ramp. The former mosque is within the 15,058-hectare (37,210-acre) Samarra Archaeological City UNESCO World Heritage Site, listed in 2007.

landmarks.name: Ziggurat of Ur
landmarks.writeup: An ancient Sumerian ziggurat located near Nasiriyah, dating back to the 21st century BCE.

wiki.extract: The Ziggurat of Ur is a Neo-Sumerian ziggurat in what was the city of Ur near Nasiriyah, in present-day Dhi Qar Province, Iraq. The structure was built during the Early Bronze Age by King Ur-Nammu of the Third Dynasty of Ur. It had crumbled to ruins by the 6th century BC of the Neo-Babylonian period, when it was restored by King Nabonidus.

cultural_events.name: Nowruz
cultural_events.writeup: The Kurdish New Year celebrated on the spring equinox with traditional music, dancing, and festivities.

wiki.extract: Nowruz is New Year's Day on the Iranian calendars, including the currently used Solar Hijri calendar. Historically, it has been observed by Iranian peoples, but is now celebrated by many Persianate cultures worldwide. It is a festival based on the Northern Hemisphere spring equinox, and thus usually coincides with a date between 19 March and 22 March on the Gregorian calendar.

cultural_events.name: Ashura
cultural_events.writeup: A significant religious observance for Shia Muslims commemorating the martyrdom of Imam Hussein.

wiki.extract: Ashura, also more formally as the Day of Ashura, is a day of commemoration in Islam. It occurs annually on the tenth of Muharram, the first month of the Islamic calendar.

cultural_events.name: Baghdad International Film Festival
cultural_events.writeup: An event showcasing regional and international films, promoting cultural exchange.

wiki.extract: Baghdad Messi is a 2023 drama film directed by Sahim Omar Kalifa, with a screenplay by Kobe Van Steenberghe from a story by Kobe Van Steenberghe and Ruth Mallaerts. It is about an Iraqi boy who, after losing his leg in a terrorist attack, fights to continue pursuing his passion for soccer. It is based on the 2012 short film of the same name by the same director. It is a co-production between Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany and Iraq.

food_writeup: Iraqi cuisine features rich flavors with staples like rice, lamb, and dates. Popular dishes include Masgouf (grilled fish), Dolma (stuffed vegetables), and Kebabs, reflecting a blend of Arab, Kurdish, and Mesopotamian culinary traditions.
brief_history: Iraq, historically known as Mesopotamia, is one of the world's earliest cradles of civilization. It has been home to ancient empires such as the Sumerians, Babylonians, and Assyrians. In modern times, Iraq was part of the Ottoman Empire before becoming a kingdom and later a republic. The country has experienced significant conflict, including the Iran-Iraq War, Gulf War, and the 2003 US-led invasion.
current_conflicts: Iraq faces ongoing security challenges including insurgent attacks, sectarian violence, and tensions with various militant groups despite efforts to stabilize the country.

commentary.inflation_management: Iraq's inflation history is a war story: 53.2% in 2006 at the height of sectarian conflict, collapsing to 2.7% by 2008 as security improved, and staying near zero through most of the 2010s under the dinar's de facto dollar peg. The December 2020 devaluation (from 1,190 to 1,460 per dollar) pushed inflation to 6.0% in 2021 and 5.0% in 2022, but it has since fallen to a projected 0.3% in 2025. The Central Bank of Iraq has kept the peg through ISIS, oil crashes, and political crises, prioritizing exchange-rate stability over an active inflation target.
commentary.debt_management: Public debt has swung violently with war and oil: it started at 143.2% of GDP in 2006 (legacy Saddam-era arrears), fell to 27.6% by 2014 as oil revenues and Paris Club relief worked through, then jumped to 60.3% in 2016 after the ISIS war and oil-price collapse, and to 72.5% in 2020 on COVID and the oil crash. Recovery brought it to a projected 53.9% in 2025. GDP swung from $65.1bn (2006) to $288.1bn (2022) with oil prices. The debt is manageable when oil is high and dangerous when it is not; there is no stabilization fund worthy of the name.

key_events.event: Sectarian civil war peak; inflation 53.2% and debt 143.2% of GDP.
Security 'surge' and oil recovery; inflation collapsed and debt began falling.
ISIS seized Mosul and oil prices crashed; debt began climbing again.
Battle for Mosul; fiscal strain peaked with debt at 60.3%.
Protests toppled the government; COVID and the oil crash pushed debt to 72.5%.
Dinar devalued to 1,460 per dollar to close the fiscal gap.
Oil windfall repaired finances; GDP hit $288.1bn.

commentary.outlook_next_decade: Iraq's outlook is an oil-price forecast with political risk attached: high prices mean surpluses and falling debt, low prices mean renewed fiscal crisis, and the historical pattern favors the latter arriving eventually. Diversification away from oil remains rhetorical, the public wage bill keeps growing, and political fragmentation blocks reform. Water scarcity and climate stress add a slow-burn risk. Analytical assessment: expect repeated boom-bust cycles with debt ratcheting higher each time unless a stabilization mechanism is built.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
